rv.q: Unfortunately, wives who remain dishrags for their husband have gone out of style at least a generation ago and her hero is so obnoxious that we don’t understand why Diana put up with him for a quarter of a century.
Fifty years ago, the marital revelations and commentary on gender roles as depicted in Art of Leaving might be considered titillating and risqué.
Art of Leaving falls short of poignantly realizing the journey of a middle-aged wife leaving her cartoonishly undeserving husband.
Watching a woman’s self-esteem get battered for 90 minutes, while being asked to find her travails amusing, is an experience that many may find masochistic.
There’s not much art here, but the desire to leave remains.
I would give this one big cringe.
The Art of Leaving is playing a limited engagement now through December 14th at the Alice Griffin Jewel Box Theatre/Pershing Square Signature Center, 480 W. 42nd Street, NYC.
But even the sharpest direction couldn’t improve this script, as irredeemable as Aaron himself.

cn.t: Critics largely pan Art of Leaving as a dated, clichéd throwback to mid-century domestic comedy, with Lucas's script faulted for tone-deaf gender politics. The elegant set earns rare praise amid otherwise harsh notices.
